tasks.title: Postgres: CAST(x AS "char") is parsed as CHAR, so the one-byte "char" type becomes bpchar
tasks.issue:
Postgres: CAST(x AS "char") is parsed as CHAR, so the one-byte "char" type becomes bpchar

- Read dialect: `postgres`
- Write dialect: `postgres`
- Still reproduces on `main` at `45158c35c`

`CAST(x AS "char")` is parsed as `CHAR`, so PostgreSQL's one-byte `"char"` becomes `bpchar` — a different type that answers the same cast with a different value.

```
input:    SELECT CAST(65 AS "char")     -- PostgreSQL: A
emitted:  SELECT CAST(65 AS CHAR)       -- PostgreSQL: 6
```

This is narrower than "quoted type names should not be resolved". Resolving them is deliberate and tested — `tests/dialects/test_postgres.py:977` asserts `1::"int"` becomes `CAST(1 AS INT)`. `"char"` is the one PostgreSQL type name where quoting changes *which type is named*, so it is the case that normalization cannot cover.

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

print(sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT CAST(a AS "char") FROM t', read="postgres").sql(dialect="postgres"))
# SELECT CAST(a AS CHAR) FROM t
```

The tokenizer keeps the two apart; the resolution happens in the parser:

```python
from sqlglot.dialects.postgres import Postgres

tok = Postgres().tokenizer_class()
print([(t.token_type.name, t.text) for t in tok.tokenize('"char"')])   # [('IDENTIFIER', 'char')]
print([(t.token_type.name, t.text) for t in tok.tokenize('char')])     # [('CHAR', 'char')]
```

**On PostgreSQL 17.10**

`"char"` is a one-byte internal type; unquoted `char` is `bpchar`. Neither cast raises, so the substitution is silent.

| statement | result |
|---|---|
| `SELECT CAST(65 AS "char")` | `A` |
| `SELECT CAST(65 AS CHAR)` — emitted | `6` |
| `SELECT pg_typeof(CAST(65 AS "char"))` | `"char"` |
| `SELECT pg_typeof(CAST(65 AS CHAR))` | `character` |
| `SELECT typname, typlen FROM pg_type WHERE typname IN ('char','bpchar')` | `char` → `1`, `bpchar` → `-1` |

**Why `"char"` is special rather than arbitrary**

Quoting suppresses keyword aliasing, so a quoted type name resolves against `pg_type.typname` literally and case-sensitively:

| written | result |
|---|---|
| `CAST(1 AS "char")` | `"char"` — the one-byte type |
| `CAST(1 AS "text")` | `text` |
| `CAST(1 AS "int4")` | `integer` |
| `CAST(1 AS "bpchar")` | `character` |
| `CAST(1 AS "int")` | `ERROR: type "int" does not exist` |
| `CAST(1 AS "integer")` | `ERROR: type "integer" does not exist` |
| `CAST(65 AS "CHAR")` | `ERROR: type "CHAR" does not exist` |

`int` and `integer` are grammar keywords aliasing `int4`; neither is a `typname`, so their quoted spellings do not resolve. Only names actually in `pg_type` work — and `char` is one, denoting the one-byte type rather than `bpchar`.

**Where it happens**

`Parser._parse_types` (`sqlglot/parser.py:6489`) re-tokenizes the identifier's *name*, which has already had its quotes stripped, and matches the result against `TYPE_TOKENS`:

```python
identifier = allow_identifiers and self._parse_id_var(any_token=False, tokens=(TokenType.VAR,))
if isinstance(identifier, exp.Identifier):
    try:
        tokens = self.dialect.tokenize(identifier.name)   # "char" -> char -> TokenType.CHAR
    except TokenError:
        tokens = None

    if tokens and (type_token := tokens[0].token_type) in self.TYPE_TOKENS:
        ...
    elif self.dialect.SUPPORTS_USER_DEFINED_TYPES:
        this = self._parse_user_defined_type(identifier)
```

`identifier.args["quoted"]` is available and not consulted, so a quoted name takes the same path as an unquoted one. For every type name but `"char"` that is the intended normalization.

**A possible fix**

Disabling the normalization wholesale breaks `test_postgres.py::test_postgres`, `test_redshift.py::test_cast` and `test_clickhouse.py::test_clickhouse`, which assert it. A dialect-declared exception list keeps those and fixes this one:

```python
# sqlglot/parser.py, on Parser
QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD: t.ClassVar[set] = set()

# in _parse_types
if (
    identifier.name not in self.QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD
    or not identifier.args.get("quoted")
) and tokens and (type_token := tokens[0].token_type) in self.TYPE_TOKENS:
    ...

# sqlglot/parsers/postgres.py, on PostgresParser
QUOTED_TYPES_DISTINCT_FROM_KEYWORD: t.ClassVar[set] = {"char"}
```

The quoted name then falls through to `_parse_user_defined_type`, which already round-trips it verbatim. On `main` at `45158c35c` this preserves `CAST(1 AS "char")`, still normalizes `CAST(1 AS "int")` to `CAST(1 AS INT)`, leaves unquoted spellings and other dialects unchanged, and `tests/test_parser.py` and `tests/dialects/` pass — 843 tests, 11545 subtests — with one pre-existing environment failure (`TestDialect::test_lazy_load`, which shells out to a `python` executable) that fails identically without the change.

**Official Documentation**

- PostgreSQL [Special Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-character.html) — `"char"` is one byte; `character(n)`/`bpchar` is blank-padded.
- PostgreSQL [Identifiers and Key Words](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-SYNTAX-IDENTIFIERS) — a quoted identifier is never a key word.

---

*Investigated with LLM assistance. The reproductions, the patched test-suite run, and the PostgreSQL 17.10 results were run against `main` at `45158c35c`.*

tasks.issue:
Snowflake: FILTER over an anonymous aggregate raises AttributeError ('str' object has no attribute 'copy')

Rewriting a `FILTER (WHERE ...)` over an anonymous aggregate to Snowflake crashes with a raw `AttributeError`.

```python
import sqlglot

sqlglot.transpile("SELECT COLLECT_LIST(x) FILTER (WHERE x = 5) FROM t", write="snowflake")
# AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'copy'
```

Named aggregates work:

```python
sqlglot.transpile("SELECT ARRAY_AGG(x) FILTER (WHERE x > 0) FROM t", write="snowflake")
# ["SELECT ARRAY_AGG(IFF(x > 0, x, NULL)) FROM t"]
```

Snowflake has no `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, so `filter_sql` rewrites the values into `IFF(cond, value, NULL)`. It reads the value from `agg.this`, but for an anonymous aggregate like `COLLECT_LIST(x)` that is the function-name string (`'COLLECT_LIST'`); the argument is in `agg.expressions`. Wrapping the string then raises.

**Expected**

`SELECT COLLECT_LIST(IFF(x = 5, x, NULL)) FROM t`, consistent with the named-aggregate case.

sqlglot 30.17.0.

tasks.title: DuckDB/SQLite: a JSON key containing an apostrophe raises TokenError, losing the statement
tasks.issue:
DuckDB/SQLite: a JSON key containing an apostrophe raises TokenError, losing the statement

- Read dialect: `duckdb`, `sqlite`
- Write dialect: n/a — the failure is on input, before any generation
- Still reproduces on `main` at `a60171e8`

A JSON key containing an apostrophe raises `TokenError` during parsing, so the whole statement is lost. The input is valid SQL in both dialects and the apostrophe is escaped correctly.

```
input:    SELECT a -> 'it''s' FROM t     -- valid DuckDB and SQLite; the key is: it's
raised:   sqlglot.errors.TokenError: Error tokenizing 'it''
expected: parses, with the key preserved
```

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT a -> 'it''s' FROM t", read="duckdb")
```

```
sqlglot.errors.TokenError: Error tokenizing 'it''
```

Same for `read="sqlite"`.

The SQL tokenizer handles the literal correctly anywhere else, which isolates it to the JSON path re-read:

```python
import sqlglot

print(sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT 'it''s' FROM t", read="duckdb").sql(dialect="duckdb"))
# SELECT 'it''s' FROM t
```

It fails only where the literal is the operand of `->` / `->>`.

**Where it comes from**

`Dialect.to_json_path` (`sqlglot/dialects/dialect.py:1171`) already has a fallback for an operand that is not a JSON path — warn, and return the literal unchanged:

```python
            try:
                return parse_json_path(path_text, self)
            except ParseError as e:
                if self.STRICT_JSON_PATH_SYNTAX and not path_text.lstrip().startswith(
                    ("lax", "strict")
                ):
                    logger.warning(f"Invalid JSON path syntax. {str(e)}")

        return path
```

`JSONPathTokenizer` raises `TokenError`, which derives from `SqlglotError` directly rather than from `ParseError`, so it escapes this handler and aborts the parse instead of falling back.

DuckDB shows the intent most clearly: it sets `STRICT_JSON_PATH_SYNTAX = False` (`sqlglot/dialects/duckdb.py:25`) to relax exactly this kind of operand, and still fails, because the exception escapes before the flag is consulted.

The tokenizer raises because it maps `'` to `QUOTE` with `STRING_ESCAPES = ["\\"]` (`sqlglot/jsonpath.py:14`), and `path.name` has already been unescaped by the SQL tokenizer — so `'it''s'` arrives as `it's` and the apostrophe opens a string that is never closed.

Widening the except clause makes both dialects parse, and the operand stays a plain literal so it round-trips with the escaping intact:

```diff
-            except ParseError as e:
+            except (ParseError, TokenError) as e:
```

```
unpatched   duckdb   TokenError          patched   SELECT a -> 'it''s' FROM t
            sqlite   TokenError                    SELECT a -> 'it''s' FROM t
```

I have not opened a PR, per the new-contributor guidance in CONTRIBUTING.

**Related**

#3185 was the same fallback failing on a `ParseError` it did catch (a `-` in a key), and was fixed. This is the sibling exception class that still escapes it. The apostrophe issues fixed so far — #4090, #8108, #8114 — are all about the generated path literal rather than the parser.

**Official Documentation**

- DuckDB [JSON functions](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/data/json/json_functions) — `->` takes a JSON path.
- SQLite [path arguments](https://sqlite.org/json1.html#path_arguments) and [string literals](https://sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#literal_values_constants_) — `''` escapes a literal apostrophe, and a path key may hold arbitrary characters.

tasks.title: Presto/Trino: singular ROW in FETCH FIRST n ROW ONLY / OFFSET n ROW fails to parse (tokenized as STRUCT)
tasks.issue:
Presto/Trino: singular ROW in FETCH FIRST n ROW ONLY / OFFSET n ROW fails to parse (tokenized as STRUCT)

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

for sql in [
    "SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY",
    "SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH NEXT 1 ROW WITH TIES",
    "SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x OFFSET 1 ROW FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY",
    "SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST ROW ONLY",
]:
    try:
        print(sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="trino").sql("trino"))
    except sqlglot.ParseError as e:
        print(e)
```

With sqlglot 30.19.0 and `read="trino"` (also `"presto"` and `"athena"`), the first three fail:

```
Invalid expression / Unexpected token. Line 1, Col: 44.
  SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
```

The last one parses but produces invalid SQL:

```
SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST ROW ROWS ONLY
```

The plural form works (`FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS ONLY`), and the default, `postgres` and `oracle` dialects parse all four statements.

Expected: all four parse and round-trip. Trino's grammar is `OFFSET count [ ROW | ROWS ]` and `FETCH { FIRST | NEXT } [ count ] { ROW | ROWS } { ONLY | WITH TIES }` ([docs](https://trino.io/docs/current/sql/select.html#offset-clause)), and `FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY` runs on Trino. We hit it in production Trino queries.

**Cause**

The Presto tokenizer maps `"ROW": TokenType.STRUCT` (for the `ROW(...)` type and constructor), so `ROW` never arrives as `TokenType.ROW`:

- `_parse_limit_options` and `_parse_offset` match only `(TokenType.ROW, TokenType.ROWS)`, so a singular `ROW` is left over and parsing fails;
- `FETCH_TOKENS` excludes `ROW` / `ROWS` but not `STRUCT`, so in `FETCH FIRST ROW ONLY` the `ROW` is taken as the count, and the output gains an extra `ROWS`.

tasks.title: ClickHouse: GLOBAL JOIN after an ON condition raises TypeError with sqlglot[c], silently loses GLOBAL in pure Python
tasks.issue:
ClickHouse: GLOBAL JOIN after an ON condition raises TypeError with sqlglot[c], silently loses GLOBAL in pure Python

### ClickHouse: `GLOBAL <kind> JOIN` right after an `ON` condition fails (`TypeError` with `sqlglot[c]`, GLOBAL silently dropped in pure Python)

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

sql = "SELECT * FROM t AS a JOIN s AS b ON a.id = b.id GLOBAL LEFT JOIN u AS c ON a.id = c.id"
print(sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="clickhouse").sql("clickhouse"))
```

With `sqlglot[c]` 30.19.0:

```
  File "sqlglot/parser.py", line 4730, in _parse_join
  File "sqlglot/parser.py", line 6054, in _parse_disjunction
  ...
  File "sqlglot/parser.py", line 6105, in _parse_range
  File "sqlglot/parsers/clickhouse.py", line 428, in <lambda>
  File "sqlglot/parsers/clickhouse.py", line 642, in _parse_global_in
TypeError: sqlglot.expressions.core.In object expected; got None
```

With the pure Python build it parses, but the second join loses `GLOBAL`:

```
SELECT * FROM t AS a JOIN s AS b ON a.id = b.id LEFT JOIN u AS c ON a.id = c.id
```

Expected: the query round-trips unchanged, as it does when the preceding join uses `USING` instead of `ON` (`... GLOBAL LEFT JOIN s AS b USING (id) GLOBAL INNER JOIN ...` works).

This happens with every join kind after `GLOBAL` (`GLOBAL JOIN`, `GLOBAL LEFT JOIN`, `GLOBAL ANY LEFT JOIN`, `GLOBAL FULL OUTER JOIN`, ...), as long as the previous join ends with an `ON` expression. It is valid ClickHouse syntax ([docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/en/sql-reference/operators/in#distributed-subqueries)) that we see in production queries.

**Cause**

`ClickHouseParser.RANGE_PARSERS` maps `TokenType.GLOBAL` to `_parse_global_in`. While parsing the `ON` condition, `_parse_range` sees the `GLOBAL` of the next join, matches it and calls `_parse_global_in`. No `IN` follows, so it returns `None` although it is annotated `-> exp.Not | exp.In`:

- the mypyc build enforces the return type and raises `TypeError`;
- in pure Python, `_parse_range` gets `None` and returns `this`, but `GLOBAL` has already been consumed, so `_parse_join_parts` never sees it and the join is parsed as non-global.

tasks.title: Postgres: JSON_VALUE with RETURNING fails to parse
tasks.issue:
Postgres: JSON_VALUE with RETURNING fails to parse

`JSON_VALUE` with a `RETURNING` clause fails to parse in the Postgres dialect. Postgres 17 supports the clause.

```python
>>> import sqlglot
>>> sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT JSON_VALUE(j, '$.a' RETURNING BIGINT) FROM t", read="postgres")
sqlglot.errors.ParseError: Expecting ). Line 1, Col: 36.
```

Without `RETURNING`, `JSON_VALUE` parses as `exp.Anonymous`.

Registering `JSON_VALUE` with the base `_parse_json_value` makes it parse, but the path then goes through `to_json_path`, and the Postgres generator renders `JSONPath` in the key-only form used by `->` and `#>`. The path is lost on the round trip:

```
SELECT JSON_VALUE(j, '$.a' RETURNING BIGINT)  ->  SELECT JSON_VALUE(j, 'a' RETURNING BIGINT)
```

Making the Postgres generator emit a full jsonpath instead is not lossless either: the default rendering turns `'$."my key"'` into `'$["my key"]'`, which Postgres reads as an array accessor and silently returns NULL for in lax mode. So I'd keep the path as written, like Trino's `_parse_json_query` does. I have a small patch along those lines with tests (every query run on Postgres 17) and can open a PR if that approach works for you.

Not covered by it: `PASSING`, and other dialects transpiling `JSON_VALUE` into Postgres (MySQL `'$.a.b'` still comes out as `'ab'`).

Found through apache/superset#36954, where a Postgres virtual dataset using this clause is rejected.

tasks.title: (bug): sqlglot corrupts PostgreSQL Unicode escape string literals (U&'...')
tasks.issue:
(bug): sqlglot corrupts PostgreSQL Unicode escape string literals (U&'...')

**Fully reproducible code snippet**
sqlglot misparses U& as identifier U + bitwise AND &, adding spaces during SQL regeneration.

Here is a snippet to test this behaviour:

```python
dialect = "postgres"
sql_original = """
    SELECT
        (U&'\FE01' || 'Test literal') AS label
    FROM data
"""
sql_transpiled = sqlglot.transpile(
    sql_original, read=dialect, write=dialect, pretty=True
)[0]

print(sql_transpiled)
```

Full output:

```
SyntaxWarning: "\F" is an invalid escape sequence. Such sequences will not work in the future. Did you mean "\\F"? A raw string is also an option.
  (U&'\FE01' || 'Test literal') AS label
SELECT
  (
    U & '\FE01' || 'Test literal'
  ) AS label
FROM data
```

**Official Documentation**
PostgreSQL [documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#:~:text=A%20variant%20of%20quoted%20identifiers%20allows%20including%20escaped%20Unicode%20characters%20identified%20by%20their%20code%20points%2E) part about escaped Unicode characters in string literals.

> This variant starts with U& (upper or lower case U followed by ampersand) immediately before the opening double quote, without any spaces in between, for example U&"foo". (Note that this creates an ambiguity with the operator &. Use spaces around the operator to avoid this problem.) Inside the quotes, Unicode characters can be specified in escaped form by writing a backslash followed by the four-digit hexadecimal code point number or alternatively a backslash followed by a plus sign followed by a six-digit hexadecimal code point number. For example, the identifier "data" could be written as `U&"d\0061t\+000061"`

tasks.title: Fail to parse duckdb's `from-first` syntax with `pivot` and join in subquery
tasks.issue:
Fail to parse duckdb's `from-first` syntax with `pivot` and join in subquery

This fails:
```python
import sqlglot

sqlglot.parse_one("""
pivot (
    from tbl_1 left join tbl_2 using (id)
    select *
)
on col_1
using sum(col_2)
""", read='duckdb')
```

Remove `select *` in the subquery, or move `select` to beginning works.

tasks.title: Temp tables not parsed correctly using tsql dialect when using quoted identifiers
tasks.issue:
Temp tables not parsed correctly using tsql dialect when using quoted identifiers

https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/issues/3399 - describes how quoted temp tables work with Microsoft tsql.

To use a Microsoft SQL Server temporary table with a name that requires quoting (such as when it contains spaces or reserved characters), you must place the # symbol inside the square brackets: [#Table Name]

The SQL below when parsed has no temporary attribute.

```
>>> exp = sg.parse_one("select name from [#temp_table]", dialect="tsql")
>>> exp
Select(
  expressions=[
    Column(
      this=Identifier(this=name, quoted=False))],
  from_=From(
    this=Table(
      this=Identifier(this='#temp_table', quoted=True))))
```
sqlglot will set a temporary attribute when the # character shows up outside the quoted brackets, but this is invalid tsql.

```
>>> exp = sg.parse_one("select name from #[temp_table]", dialect="tsql")
>>> exp
Select(
  expressions=[
    Column(
      this=Identifier(this=name, quoted=False))],
  from_=From(
    this=Table(
      this=Identifier(this='temp_table', quoted=True, temporary=True))))
```

Using the example from: https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/issues/3399

You can't round trip from duckdb to tsql and back to duckdb.

```
>>> exp = sg.parse_one("CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE 'temptest' (name VARCHAR);", dialect="duckdb")

>>> exp
Create(
  this=Schema(
    this=Table(
      this=Identifier(this='temptest', quoted=True)),
    expressions=[
      ColumnDef(
        this=Identifier(this=name, quoted=False),
        kind=DataType(this=Type.TEXT, nested=False))]),
  kind=TABLE,
  properties=Properties(
    expressions=[
      TemporaryProperty()]))

>>> exp.sql(dialect="tsql")
'CREATE TABLE [#temptest] (name VARCHAR(MAX))'

>>> ## No temporary attribute below..
>>> exp = sg.parse_one("CREATE TABLE [#temptest] (name VARCHAR(MAX))", dialect="tsql")

>>> exp
Create(
  this=Schema(
    this=Table(
      this=Identifier(this='#temptest', quoted=True)),
    expressions=[
      ColumnDef(
        this=Identifier(this=name, quoted=False),
        kind=DataType(
          this=Type.VARCHAR,
          expressions=[
            DataTypeParam(
              this=Var(this=MAX))],
          nested=False))]),
  kind=TABLE)

>>> exp.sql(dialect="duckdb")
'CREATE TABLE "#temptest" (name TEXT(MAX))'
```

tasks.title: BigQuery: FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME mis-parses FULL as an alias, causing infinite recursion in qualify()
tasks.issue:
BigQuery: FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME mis-parses FULL as an alias, causing infinite recursion in qualify()

**Before you file an issue**
- Read dialect: `bigquery` (explicit below)
- Write dialect: `bigquery` (explicit below)
- Reproduces on current `main` (`b4c9ad5`, 2026-08-16, `30.17.1.dev26`)

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify

sql = "WITH c AS ((SELECT a FROM t1) FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME (SELECT a FROM t2)) SELECT * FROM c"
tree = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="bigquery")
qualify(tree, dialect="bigquery", validate_qualify_columns=False)
```

Raises `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded` on pure Python. On the compiled `sqlglot[c]` build the same unbounded recursion runs in native frames and segfaults the process instead (uncatchable, exit -11) rather than raising — I didn't reproduce that half myself this time, but it's the expected consequence of infinite recursion in a mypyc-compiled function and matches the same failure shape as #7732.

**Root cause — parser mis-parses `FULL` as an implicit alias**

```python
>>> sqlglot.parse_one("(SELECT a FROM t1) FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME (SELECT a FROM t2)", read="bigquery")
Union(
  this=Alias(
    this=Subquery(this=Select(...FROM t1)),
    alias=Identifier(this=FULL, quoted=False)),   # <- "FULL" consumed as an alias, not as "FULL OUTER"
  distinct=False,
  by_name=True,
  expression=Subquery(this=Select(...FROM t2)),
  kind=OUTER)                                       # only "OUTER" survives as the union kind
```

`FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME` is BigQuery's `FULL OUTER` set-operator syntax (see docs link below) — `FULL` and `OUTER` belong together as one modifier on the union itself. Instead, the parser treats the left subquery as implicitly aliased `AS FULL` (valid in isolation — `(SELECT ...) FULL` alone parses as an aliased subquery), and only `OUTER` is left to attach to the union's `kind`. This produces a tree where the union's left operand is an `Alias`, not a `Query`.

That malformed tree then hits `Scope.external_columns` (`sqlglot/optimizer/scope.py:474`):

```python
if isinstance(self.expression, exp.SetOperation):
    left, right = self.union_scopes
    self._external_columns = left.external_columns + right.external_columns
```

I traced the recursion with a lowered `sys.setrecursionlimit()` — the entire stack is `external_columns` calling itself at line 474, over and over. The scope built by `_traverse_union` for the `Alias`-wrapped operand ends up structured so that walking into `union_scopes` loops back into a scope that again satisfies `isinstance(self.expression, exp.SetOperation)`, so it never reaches the `else` branch that would actually compute and terminate.

This is likely related to `_traverse_union`'s switch (in the same file, ~line 780) from type-checked `.left`/`.right` accessors to raw `.this`/`.expression` in a85eeff2 (#7897) — that change was needed for legitimate non-Query set-operation operands (e.g. `VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1`), and I confirmed it still works correctly. But it also removed the guard that used to reject a malformed operand like this `Alias` before it could reach `external_columns` at all.

**What I did NOT verify**: a fix. Restoring the old `.left`/`.right` accessors would just re-break the `VALUES` case #7897 fixed, and I couldn't find a guard in `_traverse_union` or `external_columns` that rejects this specific malformed shape without also rejecting legitimate operands. There may also be a parser-level fix (don't let `FULL`/`LEFT`/`INNER` be consumed as an implicit alias when followed by `OUTER UNION`/`OUTER INTERSECT`/`OUTER EXCEPT` in bigquery/dialects that support this syntax) that would prevent the malformed tree from being built in the first place, which might be the more correct place to fix this — but I didn't attempt it, since it touches parser precedence rules I'm not confident about getting right without regressing normal implicit-alias parsing. Filing with the repro and root-cause trace rather than guessing at a fix.

**Official Documentation**

BigQuery set operators (`FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME` etc.): https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#set_operators

+import unittest
+
+import sqlglot
+from sqlglot import exp
+from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify
+
+
+class TestBigQueryFullOuterUnionByName(unittest.TestCase):
+    def test_parenthesized_full_outer_union_by_name(self):
+        for side, kind in [("FULL", "OUTER"), ("LEFT", None), ("RIGHT", None)]:
+            modifier = f"{side} {kind}" if kind else side
+            sql = f"(SELECT a FROM t1) {modifier} UNION ALL BY NAME (SELECT a FROM t2)"
+            tree = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="bigquery")
+            self.assertIsInstance(tree, exp.Union)
+            self.assertNotIsInstance(tree.this, exp.Alias)
+            self.assertEqual(tree.args.get("side"), side)
+            self.assertEqual(tree.args.get("kind"), kind)
+
+    def test_full_outer_union_by_name_qualify_terminates(self):
+        sql = "WITH c AS ((SELECT a FROM t1) FULL OUTER UNION ALL BY NAME (SELECT a FROM t2)) SELECT * FROM c"
+        tree = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="bigquery")
+        qualify(tree, dialect="bigquery", validate_qualify_columns=False)
+
+    def test_implicit_full_alias_without_set_op_still_parses(self):
+        tree = sqlglot.parse_one("(SELECT a FROM t1) FULL", read="bigquery")
+        self.assertIsInstance(tree, exp.Alias)
+
+    def test_explicit_full_alias_before_union_still_parses(self):
+        tree = sqlglot.parse_one(
+            "(SELECT a FROM t1) AS FULL UNION ALL (SELECT a FROM t2)", read="bigquery"
+        )
+        self.assertIsInstance(tree, exp.Union)
+        self.assertIsInstance(tree.this, exp.Alias)
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    unittest.main()

tasks.title: eliminate_qualify selects the columns inside a moved window, and replaces a table-qualified column with a same-named alias
tasks.issue:
eliminate_qualify selects the columns inside a moved window, and replaces a table-qualified column with a same-named alias

Read dialect `snowflake`, write dialect `postgres`. Reproduced on 30.17.0; `transforms.eliminate_qualify` on `main` (8bd7686) is the same code. Every dialect whose generator runs `eliminate_qualify` is affected, including T-SQL, MySQL, Oracle, Trino, Presto, Hive, Spark and SQLite.

`eliminate_qualify` moves each window function in QUALIFY into a subquery's SELECT as `_w`, and filters on `_w` outside. Two of its steps go wrong when the window reads columns:

1. It also adds each column found inside the window to the subquery's SELECT. The subquery already computes the window, so those columns aren't needed, and adding them breaks the query when:
   - the query is grouped and the window aggregates the column, like `s` in `ORDER BY SUM(s)`: the column is selected ungrouped;
   - the window holds a subquery: its columns, like `y.s`, are selected where their table isn't in scope.
2. Before moving the window, it replaces each column inside it whose name matches a SELECT alias with that alias's expression. It checks only the name, so a column that names its table, like `x.s`, is replaced too, though it reads the table and not the alias. Beside `SUM(x.s) AS s`, `SUM(x.s)` becomes `SUM(SUM(x.s))`.

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

for sql in [
    "SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY d, c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) <= 3",
    "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) <= 3",
    "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) <= 3",
]:
    print(sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="snowflake", write="postgres")[0])
```

Output:

```
SELECT d, c, t FROM (SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) AS _w, s FROM x GROUP BY d, c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
SELECT c, s FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(SUM(x.s)) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
SELECT c, t FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) AS _w, y.s FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
```

Expected:

```
SELECT d, c, t FROM (SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY d, c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
SELECT c, s FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
SELECT c, t FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3
```

I ran both in DuckDB over the same tables `x (d INT, c VARCHAR, s INT)` and `y (c VARCHAR, s INT)`, with Postgres's null order (`SET default_null_order = 'nulls_last_on_asc_first_on_desc'`). DuckDB refuses each current output:

| Query | Error |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `Binder Error: column "s" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or must be part of an aggregate function.` |
| 2 | `Binder Error: aggregate function calls cannot be nested` |
| 3 | `Binder Error: Referenced table "y" not found!` |

Each expected output returns the same rows as `sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="snowflake", write="duckdb")`, which keeps QUALIFY.

**A possible fix**

```diff
             if isinstance(select_candidate, exp.Window):
                 if expression_by_alias:
                     for column in select_candidate.find_all(exp.Column):
                         expr = expression_by_alias.get(column.name)
-                        if expr:
+                        if expr and not column.table:
                             column.replace(expr)
@@
-            elif select_candidate.name not in expression.named_selects:
+            elif select_candidate.name not in expression.named_selects and not select_candidate.find_ancestor(exp.Window):
                 expression.select(select_candidate.copy(), copy=False)
```

With it, the queries above print as expected, and:

- A column outside any window is still selected, since the outer WHERE reads it: `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY e) = 1 AND f > 0` still adds `f`. It no longer adds `e`, which only the window reads.
- An unqualified alias inside the window is still replaced: `ORDER BY t DESC` beside `SUM(x.s) AS t` still becomes `ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC`.

**Official Documentation**

[QUALIFY](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/constructs/qualify): "In a SELECT statement, the QUALIFY clause filters the results of window functions." Its evaluation order puts QUALIFY after GROUP BY, HAVING and WINDOW, so a window in QUALIFY is computed over the grouped rows, as it would be in the SELECT list. Computing it in the subquery's SELECT needs no other column from inside it.

+import unittest
+
+import sqlglot
+
+
+class TestEliminateQualifyWindowColumns(unittest.TestCase):
+    def validate(self, sql, target):
+        with self.subTest(sql):
+            self.assertEqual(
+                sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="snowflake", write="postgres")[0],
+                target,
+            )
+
+    def test_window_columns_not_projected(self):
+        # Grouped window arg must not be added ungrouped to the subquery SELECT
+        self.validate(
+            "SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY d, c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) <= 3",
+            "SELECT d, c, t FROM (SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY d, c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+        )
+        # Table-qualified column must not be replaced by a same-named alias
+        self.validate(
+            "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) <= 3",
+            "SELECT c, s FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+        )
+        # Columns from a subquery inside the window are out of scope outside it
+        self.validate(
+            "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) <= 3",
+            "SELECT c, t FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+        )
+
+    def test_outside_window_column_still_projected(self):
+        self.validate(
+            "SELECT d FROM x QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY e) = 1 AND f > 0",
+            "SELECT d FROM (SELECT d, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY e) AS _w, f FROM x) AS _t WHERE _w = 1 AND f > 0",
+        )
+
+    def test_unqualified_alias_still_replaced(self):
+        self.validate(
+            "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY t DESC) <= 3",
+            "SELECT c, t FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+        )
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    unittest.main()

+import unittest
+

+
+
+class TestEliminateQualify(unittest.TestCase):
+    def test_window_inputs_not_projected(self):
+        cases = (
+            (
+                "SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY d, c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) <= 3",
+                "SELECT d, c, t FROM (SELECT d, c, SUM(s) AS t, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY SUM(s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY d, c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+            ),
+            (
+                "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) <= 3",
+                "SELECT c, s FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS s, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+            ),
+            (
+                "SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t FROM x GROUP BY x.c QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) <= 3",
+                "SELECT c, t FROM (SELECT x.c, SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT SUM(y.s) FROM y WHERE y.c = x.c) DESC) AS _w FROM x GROUP BY x.c) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+            ),
+        )
+        for sql, expected in cases:
+            with self.subTest(sql):
+                self.assertEqual(
+                    sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="snowflake", write="postgres")[0], expected
+                )
+

+        self.assertEqual(

+                write="postgres",
+            )[0],
+            "SELECT t FROM (SELECT SUM(x.s) AS t, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x.s) DESC) AS _w FROM x) AS _t WHERE _w <= 3",
+        )
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    unittest.main()

tasks.title: Postgres: ^@ (starts with) is parsed as POWER
tasks.issue:
Postgres: ^@ (starts with) is parsed as POWER

The Postgres dialect doesn't tokenize the starts-with operator `^@` (PG 11+), so it is read as `^` followed by `@`:

```python
import sqlglot
sqlglot.transpile("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name ^@ 'abc'", read="postgres", write="postgres")
# ["SELECT * FROM t WHERE POWER(name, $'abc')"]
sqlglot.transpile("SELECT s ^@ p FROM t", read="postgres", write="postgres")
# ['SELECT POWER(s, $p) FROM t']
```

Expected `STARTS_WITH(name, 'abc')` (or `name ^@ 'abc'`). The first output doesn't parse in Postgres; the second silently turns the column `p` into a parameter. Same result with `write="duckdb"`.

The DuckDB dialect already handles this (`"^@": TokenType.CARET_AT` in its tokenizer and `binary_range_parser(exp.StartsWith)` in its parser). Adding the same two entries to the Postgres tokenizer and `RANGE_PARSERS` fixes it locally: the Postgres test suite passes with `validate_identity("a ^@ b", "STARTS_WITH(a, b)")` added, and of the PostgreSQL regression suite's statements only the three `^@` ones change. Happy to open a PR if you'd like one.

I used Claude to find and check this.

tasks.title: logic inconsistance for CTE name with column names in sqlite
tasks.issue:
logic inconsistance for CTE name with column names in sqlite

I am using sqlglot to rewrite SQLite queries. However, sqlglot modifies the original query during a simple parse + serialize round trip, which introduces a semantic error before I even apply any rewrite logic.

Original query:
```
WITH xyz(x) AS (SELECT 1)
SELECT x FROM xyz;
```
I only perform parsing and serialization:
```
sql = """WITH xyz(x) AS (SELECT 1)
        SELECT x FROM xyz;"""

ast = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="sqlite")
print(ast.sql(dialect="sqlite"))
```
Expected output:
```
WITH xyz(x) AS (SELECT 1)
SELECT x FROM xyz;
```
Actual output:
```
WITH xyz AS (SELECT 1)
SELECT x FROM xyz;
```
The column name declaration (x) in the CTE is removed during serialization, which caused error when it was executed on sqlite.

tasks.title: PostgreSQL Unicode string generation does not re-escape apostrophes
tasks.issue:
PostgreSQL Unicode string generation does not re-escape apostrophes

﻿## Bug description

SQLGlot parses a PostgreSQL Unicode escape string containing an escaped apostrophe, but the PostgreSQL generator can emit the decoded apostrophe without doubling it again. The generated SQL is then invalid or no longer represents the same AST.

This is a generated-SQL correctness defect. The reproduction uses only a benign literal and does not execute SQL or claim a security boundary.

## Environment

- SQLGlot: upstream `main@5258f24934a0f68cb42c6698db6e4992eedeb1c9`
- Python: CPython 3.12.10 on Windows
- Surface: PostgreSQL parse -> generate -> reparse

## Reproduction

```python
from sqlglot import parse_one

expression = parse_one("SELECT U&'can''t'", read="postgres")
generated = expression.sql(dialect="postgres")
print(generated)
parse_one(generated, read="postgres")
```

At the affected base, the output is:

```text
SELECT U&'can't'
```

Reparsing the generated output raises `TokenError` because the apostrophe terminates the Unicode string early. The expected output keeps the escaped delimiter, for example `SELECT U&'can''t'`, and reparses to the same expression.

## Expected behavior

The generator should re-escape apostrophes after Unicode escape substitution so that generated PostgreSQL remains valid and preserves the parsed expression.

## Negative controls

- A Unicode string without an apostrophe round-trips normally.
- The ordinary bitwise expression `SELECT u & 5 FROM t` remains a bitwise expression.
- The local validation fix reparses the apostrophe case to an equal AST and preserves backslash and custom `UESCAPE` controls.

## Root cause and suggested fix

The shared `Generator.unicodestring_sql` method inserted decoded text between Unicode delimiters without escaping the target delimiter. The validated local fix calls the existing string escaper with `escape_backslash=False` and the selected right delimiter. This preserves Unicode escape backslashes while doubling the delimiter.

## Documentation

- PostgreSQL lexical structure and string constants: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html
- SQLGlot generator source: https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/main/sqlglot/generator.py

## Local verification

- Exact-base output/reparse failure reproduced deterministically.
- Local fix commit: `322423a0c7e2f7b6682d5442dd57b2ad5fabcb77`.
- Focused PostgreSQL test, PostgreSQL module (29 tests), relevant PostgreSQL/Presto/Oracle/generator suite (82 tests), and no-`UNICODE_START` control (26 tests) passed locally.
- Full repository CI was not run in the local worker; please run the normal project checks.

Sqlite: Multiple IN operators caused an sqlglot.errors.ParseError.

read="sqlite"
dialect="sqlite"
Confirmed on main: reproduces on commit fd6d4d61c25e7918118fc22c5579098a86a58e10

**Fully reproducible code snippet**
```python
import sqlglot
sql = "SELECT 1 NOT IN (0) IN (1)"

ast = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read = "sqlite")
```
it output:
```
sqlglot.errors.ParseError: Invalid expression / Unexpected token. Line 1, Col: 22.
  SELECT 1 NOT IN (0) IN (1)
```
This query can be successfully executed on sqlite3

tasks.title: `_traverse_union` corrupts the scope graph when a set-operation operand isn't a Query, causing infinite recursion in `qualify()` (reproducible with valid SQL: VALUES on redshift/mysql/bigquery)
tasks.issue:
`_traverse_union` corrupts the scope graph when a set-operation operand isn't a Query, causing infinite recursion in `qualify()` (reproducible with valid SQL: VALUES on redshift/mysql/bigquery)

**Before you file an issue**
- Read dialect: none required for the first repro; `redshift` / `mysql` / `bigquery` (second repro, explicit below)
- Write dialect: n/a (crashes before generating output)
- Reproduces on current `main` (`bac1a897b`, 2026-08-25, `v30.17.0-72-gbac1a897b`)

**Summary**

`_traverse_union` (`sqlglot/optimizer/scope.py`) builds a `Scope` for each set-operation operand by consuming `_traverse_scope()`'s generator in a loop. When an operand isn't one of the node types `_traverse_scope` knows how to build a scope for (not a `Select`, `SetOperation`, `Subquery`, `Table`, `UDTF`, `DDL`, or `DML`), `_traverse_scope` logs a warning and returns without yielding anything — but the calling loop doesn't check for that, and proceeds to use its loop variable unconditionally. That corrupts the `Scope` graph into a **self-referential** structure instead of raising, and `Scope.external_columns` then recurses into the cycle unboundedly:

- On pure Python this raises `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.
- On the compiled `sqlglot[c]` build, by the same mechanism reported in #7732, the same unbounded recursion is expected to run in mypyc-compiled frames that don't reliably honor Python's recursion check and crash the process (`SIGSEGV`) instead of raising. I did not reproduce that half myself (no `sqlglot[c]` build in my environment) — flagging it as expected-but-unverified, not confirmed.

This is **not limited to malformed SQL**. A lenient parse of truncated/malformed input can produce a non-Query operand, but so can ordinary, valid SQL on three dialects, via how they parse a bare `VALUES (...)`.

**Fully reproducible code snippets**

1) Malformed/truncated SQL (a parse fragment leaving a bare `Column` where a `Query` was expected):

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify

qualify(sqlglot.parse_one("a UNION SELECT 1"))
# RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

2) Valid SQL — `VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1` is the exact example already used in `_traverse_union`'s own source comment ("Access the args directly instead of the left/right properties, because set operation operands aren't guaranteed to be Query nodes, e.g. in VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1"). Most dialects parse a bare `VALUES (...)` into a synthetic `Select`, which works fine. Three dialects instead parse it as `exp.Anonymous`, which hits this bug:

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer.qualify import qualify

for dialect in ("redshift", "mysql", "bigquery"):
    qualify(sqlglot.parse_one("VALUES (1) UNION ALL SELECT 1", dialect=dialect), dialect=dialect)
    # RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

| dialect | `VALUES (1)` parses to | `qualify()` |
|---|---|---|
| `redshift` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| `mysql` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| `bigquery` | `exp.Anonymous` | **RecursionError** |
| *(none / generic)* | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `postgres` | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `snowflake` | `exp.Select` | OK |
| `duckdb` | `exp.Select` | OK |

**Root cause**

`_traverse_union`'s per-operand loop (`sqlglot/optimizer/scope.py`, currently around line 800):

```python
def _traverse_union(scope: Scope) -> Iterator[Scope]:
    ...
    while expression_stack:
        ...
        for scope in _traverse_scope(new_scope):
            yield scope

        if prev_scope:
            union_scope_stack.pop()
            union_scope.union_scopes = [prev_scope, scope]
            ...
```

`scope` here is both the loop variable **and** the function's own parameter (`def _traverse_union(scope: Scope) -> Iterator[Scope]:`). If `_traverse_scope(new_scope)` yields nothing (the "Cannot traverse scope" warning path), the `for` loop runs zero iterations, and `scope` is left bound to whatever it held *before* the loop — on the first operand processed, that's the union's own outer scope, since nothing has reassigned it yet.

That makes `prev_scope = scope` (the `else` branch, taken on the first operand) bind `prev_scope` to the union's *own* scope rather than a real operand scope. When the second (valid) operand is then processed, `union_scope.union_scopes = [prev_scope, scope]` runs with `union_scope` being that same outer scope, so this line becomes self-referential — confirmed directly:

```python
>>> from sqlglot.optimizer.scope import traverse_scope
>>> root = traverse_scope(sqlglot.parse_one("a UNION SELECT 1"))[-1]
>>> root.union_scopes[0] is root
True
```

`Scope.external_columns` (`scope.py`, ~line 474) recurses through `union_scopes` and only memoizes its result *after* the recursive call returns:

```python
if self._external_columns is None:
    if isinstance(self.expression, exp.SetOperation):
        left, right = self.union_scopes
        self._external_columns = left.external_columns + right.external_columns  # assigned AFTER both calls return
```

so `self._external_columns` stays `None` throughout the descent, and the `left is self` cycle recurses without ever reaching the memo guard.

**Related issues**

This is the same downstream mechanism (self-referential `union_scopes` -> unbounded `external_columns` recursion) as #8195, reached through a different malformed-operand shape. I confirmed this directly by hand-constructing #8195's exact `Alias`-wrapped-`Subquery` operand tree and running it through `traverse_scope`/`external_columns` on current `main`: it hits the identical warning (`Cannot traverse scope ... with type 'Alias'`), the identical self-reference (`union_scopes[0] is root`), and the identical `RecursionError`. #8195 was closed by a parser-level fix (a570cf8a) that stops BigQuery from mis-parsing `FULL` as an alias in that one specific construct — which prevents that particular malformed tree from being built, but doesn't touch `_traverse_union` itself, so the general failure mode is still reachable through any other route to a non-Query operand, including the two above.

(#7732 is a different bug, in `resolver.py`'s column-type resolution for `LATERAL FLATTEN`/`UNNEST`, unrelated to this one beyond sharing the same "RecursionError in pure Python, expected SIGSEGV in `sqlglot[c]`" failure shape.)

**Fix**

I have a fix ready: give the loop its own variable, and raise `OptimizeError` immediately if `_traverse_scope` yields nothing for an operand instead of proceeding with a corrupted graph. `_traverse_ctes` in the same file already handles the equivalent situation correctly (initializes `child_scope: Scope | None = None` before its loop and checks `if child_scope:` after) — a good existing reference for the pattern. Full test suite passes locally (1239 passed, 19363 subtests) with a new regression test covering both cases above. Will link the PR here once it's up.

tasks.title: Teradata: window aggregates with ORDER BY and no frame clause silently become running totals when transpiled
tasks.issue:
Teradata: window aggregates with ORDER BY and no frame clause silently become running totals when transpiled

**Before you file an issue**
- Read dialect: `teradata`
- Write dialect: `snowflake` (also reproduces with `duckdb`, `postgres` and other ANSI-default targets)
- Reproduced on `main` @ `a00dc2e5c`

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

sql = "SELECT p, d, x, SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d) AS s FROM t"
for w in ("snowflake", "duckdb", "postgres"):
    print(w, sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="teradata", write=w)[0])
```

Current output (identical for all three targets):
```sql
SELECT p, d, x, SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d NULLS FIRST) AS s FROM t
```

In Teradata, a window aggregate that has `ORDER BY` but no `ROWS` clause covers the **whole partition**. ANSI-default engines such as Snowflake, DuckDB and Postgres use `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which is a **running total**. The query transpiles without error, but it silently returns different numbers.

For rows `(p='A', d=1, x=10), ('A', 2, 20), ('A', 3, 30)`:

| d | Teradata `s` | Transpiled `s` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60 | 10 |
| 2 | 60 | 30 |
| 3 | 60 | 60 |

**Expected output** (Snowflake, for example):
```sql
SELECT p, d, x, SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d NULLS FIRST ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS s FROM t
```

**Scope**
- Teradata's docs list the affected window aggregates: AVG, CORR, COUNT, COVAR_POP/SAMP, MAX, MIN, REGR_*, STDDEV_POP/SAMP, SUM, VAR_POP/SAMP.
- The docs say `FIRST_VALUE`/`LAST_VALUE` have a different default, so they need separate handling.
- Ranking and navigation functions (`ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `LAG`, `LEAD`, …) take no frame and aren't affected.
- Windows without `ORDER BY` already cover the whole partition in every engine, so they're unaffected.

**Possible approach**
When the Teradata parser reads an aggregate window that has `ORDER BY` and no frame, it could attach an explicit `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`. The Teradata generator could then leave that default frame out, so Teradata→Teradata round trips stay unchanged.

**Official Documentation**
- Teradata, *The Window Specification → ANSI Compliance*: https://docs.teradata.com/r/Enterprise_IntelliFlex_VMware/SQL-Functions-Expressions-and-Predicates/Ordered-Analytical/Window-Aggregate-Functions/The-Window-Specification/ANSI-Compliance. Key line: "Teradata SQL window aggregate functions use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING."
- Snowflake, *Window function syntax and usage*: https://docs.snowflake.com/sql-reference/functions-window-syntax

tasks.title: Snowflake: `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*)` fails to parse
tasks.issue:
Snowflake: `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*)` fails to parse

**Dialect:** read `snowflake`, write `snowflake`.
**Version:** reproduces on `main` (`bac1a89`).

**Disclaimer:** LLMs were used to investigate this issue, write up the script for reproducibility and propose a fix. I verified all findings locally. I've collapsed information into `details` blocks as well to avoid an extremely long issue.


# Summary

Snowflake lets you qualify the wildcard argument of `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL` with a
table name or alias. This is the same behaviour as the `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT()` function, except it builds an `OBJECT` from every column of that row, keeping the `NULL`-valued keys. sqlglot parses the unqualified form but raises on the qualified one:

**Input SQL** (dialect `snowflake`):

```sql
SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*) FROM tbl AS t
```

**Expected output:** the same SQL back, as `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.*)` already round-trips.

**Actual output + reproduction:**

```python
import sqlglot

# ok
sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.*) FROM tbl AS t", read="snowflake").sql(dialect="snowflake")
# 'SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.*) FROM tbl AS t'

# ok
sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(*) FROM tbl AS t", read="snowflake").sql(dialect="snowflake")
# 'SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(*) FROM tbl AS t'

# ParseError
sqlglot.parse_one("SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*) FROM tbl AS t", read="snowflake")

>>> sqlglot.errors.ParseError: Required keyword: 'expression' missing for
>>> <class 'sqlglot.expressions.query.JSONKeyValue'>. Line 1, Col: 38.
>>>   SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*) FROM tbl AS t
```

It isn't specific to a table alias (`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(tbl.*)` against an unaliased table fails identically), and the `ILIKE` filter form is affected the same way.

| argument | `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` | `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(*)` | `StarMap` | `JSONObject` |
| `(t.*)` | `StarMap` | **ParseError** |
| `(* ILIKE 'col1%')` | `StarMap` | `JSONObject` |
| `(t.* ILIKE 'col1%')` | `StarMap` | **ParseError** |
| `('a', 1)` | `Struct` | `JSONObject` |

# Official Documentation

- [`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL`](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/object_construct_keep_null) regarding the `*` argument: 

> "When you pass a wildcard to the function, you can qualify the  wildcard with the name or alias for the table. For example, to pass in all of the columns  from the table named `mytable`, specify the following: `(mytable.*)`". 

The same section  documents `(* ILIKE 'col1%')` and `(* EXCLUDE col1)`, and notes "Qualifiers are valid when
you use these keywords", with `(mytable.* ILIKE 'col1%')` as the example.

- [`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT`](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/functions/object_construct), which has identical wildcard argument rules. sqlglot already parses this correctly.

# Details

### Root cause

`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` goes through `build_object_construct`, which handles both unqualified and qualified `*` fine. 

`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL` goes through `_parse_json_object()`, which only handles unqualified `*`, otherwise falling back to key-value pair parsing (`alias.*` is then parsed as a JSON key, but it has no matching value, causing the aforementioned `ParseError`). 

<details>
<summary>Detailed root cause</summary>

`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` and `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL` are wired up through two different
mechanisms.

`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` is a `FUNCTIONS` entry ([here](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parsers/snowflake.py#L564)), and is mapped to [`build_object_construct`.](https://github.com/ishaan-upadhyay/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parsers/snowflake.py#L1403). This handles `t.*` as `Column(this=Star(), table=t)` via [`build_var_map` ](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parser.py#L51) -> [`is_star`](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parser.py#L51), which handles expressions like `t.*` fine:

```python
class Expression(Expr):

    ...
    @property
    def is_star(self) -> bool:
        return isinstance(self, Star) or (isinstance(self, Column) and isinstance(self.this, Star))
```

`OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL` is a `FUNCTION_PARSERS` entry instead, [routed to the SQL
standard `JSON_OBJECT` grammar](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parsers/snowflake.py#L740) via `_parse_json_object` (it was added that way in #2769, for #2768):

and `_parse_json_object` recognises only an *unqualified* star:

```python
# sqlglot/parser.py
def _parse_json_object(self, agg=False):
    star = self._parse_star()
    expressions = (
        [star]
        if star
        else self._parse_csv(lambda: self._parse_format_json(self._parse_json_key_value()))
    )
```

[`_parse_star()` matches a bare `TokenType.STAR` token. ](https://github.com/ishaan-upadhyay/sqlglot/blob/bac1a897bb367732792d7d244d9805cc4ad41f0d/sqlglot/parser.py#L8903)

```python
    def _parse_star(self) -> exp.Expr | None:
        if self._match(TokenType.STAR):
            return self.PRIMARY_PARSERS[TokenType.STAR](self, self._prev)
        return self._parse_placeholder()
```

On `t.*` the current token is an identifier, so parsing falls through to `_parse_json_key_value()`, which takes `t.*` as the key, finds no `:` or `,` separator, and builds a `JSONKeyValue` with no `expression`,  hence the "Required keyword" error.
</details>


### Possible fix
<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

Give the Snowflake function its own handler that matches a qualified star before falling back to the `JSON_OBJECT` grammar, leaving the ANSI `JSON_OBJECT` path untouched:

```python
     FUNCTION_PARSERS = {
         **parser.Parser.FUNCTION_PARSERS,
         "DATE_PART": lambda self: self._parse_date_part(),
         "DIRECTORY": lambda self: self._parse_directory(),
-        "OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL": lambda self: self._parse_json_object(),
+        "OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL": lambda self: self._parse_object_construct_keep_null(),
         "LISTAGG": lambda self: self._parse_string_agg(),
```

```python
    def _parse_object_construct_keep_null(self) -> exp.Expr:
        # OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(tbl.*) is valid Snowflake, as is OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(tbl.*).
        # _parse_json_object() only recognises an unqualified star, so match the
        # qualified form here before falling back to the JSON_OBJECT grammar.
        index = self._index
        column = self._parse_column()
        if column is not None and column.is_star:
            return self.expression(exp.JSONObject(expressions=[column]))

        self._retreat(index)
        return self._parse_json_object()
```

Going through `_parse_column()` also continues to allow the `ILIKE` + unqualified `*` forms. `Expression.is_star` already handles `Star()` as well as `Column(this=Star())`. The generator needs no change:

`exp.JSONObject: lambda self, e: self.func("OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL", *e.expressions)` renders the column back as `t.*`.

I ran the test suite on `main` with this change: **1238 passed, 19360 subtests passed**, identical to the unpatched suite at the same commit. 
</details>

I would be happy to submit a PR if this approach makes sense, with a `test_snowflake.py` case alongside the existing `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT` ones.


### Fully reproducible code snippet

The script below installs sqlglot from `main` and monkey-patches in the proposed fix to
demonstrate viability.

<details>
<summary>Script for reproduction + output</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env -S SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION=0 uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = [
#   "sqlglot @ https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz",
# ]
# ///
"""Repro: OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(tbl.*) fails to parse in the snowflake dialect.

Runs against main. Every case is parsed with read="snowflake" and written back
with dialect="snowflake"; "ok" means the output matched the input exactly.

Installing from the main tarball rather than git+ because the repo has a private
submodule (sqlglot-integration-tests), which makes a recursive clone fail. The
tarball carries no git metadata, hence SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION above.

Only the qualified star on the KEEP_NULL variant is affected. The unqualified
star parses, with or without ILIKE, and OBJECT_CONSTRUCT parses in every form.

Expected output:

    current
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*)                           StarMap
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.*)                         StarMap
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.* ILIKE 'col1%')           StarMap
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(*)                 JSONObject
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(* ILIKE 'col1%')   JSONObject
       ok    OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL('a', 1)            JSONObject
       FAIL  OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*)               ParseError: Required keyword: 'expression' missing ...
       FAIL  OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.* ILIKE 'col1%') ParseError: Required keyword: 'expression' missing ...

    with the proposed fix
       ... the same, with both FAILs now ok and JSONObject
"""

import sqlglot
from sqlglot import exp
from sqlglot.dialects.snowflake import Snowflake

CASES = [
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*) FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.*) FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(t.* ILIKE 'col1%') FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(*) FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(* ILIKE 'col1%') FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL('a', 1) FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.*) FROM tbl AS t",
    "SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL(t.* ILIKE 'col1%') FROM tbl AS t",
]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- proposed fix


def parse_object_construct_keep_null(self) -> exp.Expr:
    """Match a qualified star before falling back to the JSON_OBJECT grammar.

    Upstream this is a SnowflakeParser method, wired into FUNCTION_PARSERS in
    place of the current `lambda self: self._parse_json_object()`.
    """
    index = self._index
    column = self._parse_column()
    if column is not None and column.is_star:
        return self.expression(exp.JSONObject(expressions=[column]))

    self._retreat(index)
    return self._parse_json_object()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------- harness


def label(sql: str) -> str:
    return sql[len("SELECT ") : -len(" FROM tbl AS t")]


def report() -> None:
    for sql in CASES:
        try:
            ast = sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="snowflake")
        except sqlglot.errors.ParseError as e:
            print(f"   FAIL  {label(sql):<45} ParseError: {str(e).splitlines()[0]}")
            continue

        written = ast.sql(dialect="snowflake")
        node = type(ast.selects[0]).__name__
        if written == sql:
            print(f"   ok    {label(sql):<45} {node}")
        else:
            print(f"   DIFF  {label(sql):<45} {node}, wrote back {label(written)}")


print("current")
report()

# The parser looks FUNCTION_PARSERS up on the class at parse time, so replacing
# the entry is enough to swap the handler.
Snowflake.Parser.FUNCTION_PARSERS["OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL"] = parse_object_construct_keep_null

print("\nwith the proposed fix")
report()
```

tasks.title: ClickHouse: PROJECTION fails to parse as a column identifier in INSERT statements
tasks.issue:
ClickHouse: PROJECTION fails to parse as a column identifier in INSERT statements

## Description

When \`PROJECTION\` is used as a **column identifier** (backtick-quoted) inside a ClickHouse \`INSERT INTO ... SELECT\` statement, sqlglot raises a \`ParseError\` instead of treating it as a regular identifier.

## Version

sqlglot 26.13.2

## Reproduction

```python
from sqlglot import Dialects, parse_one

sql = (
    "INSERT INTO \`my_db\`.\`my_table\` (\`id\`, \`PROJECTION\`)"
    " SETTINGS log_comment = 'test'"
    " SELECT \`id\`, \`PROJECTION\` FROM \`my_source\`"
)

parse_one(sql, dialect=Dialects.CLICKHOUSE)
```

**Error:**

```
sqlglot.errors.ParseError: Expecting (. Line 1, Col: ...
```

## Expected behaviour

\`PROJECTION\` should be accepted as a quoted column identifier, consistent with how other reserved keywords are handled when backtick-quoted in ClickHouse.

## Notes

The ClickHouse dialect reserves \`PROJECTION\` for the \`PROJECTION (...)\` table constraint clause. However, ClickHouse itself allows any keyword to be used as a column name when backtick-quoted, so the parser should follow the same rule.

Workaround: replace the identifier with a placeholder before parsing and restore it after emitting. Happy to contribute a fix if the approach is confirmed.

```
ParseError Required keyword: 'this' missing for <class 'sqlglot.expressions.query.Where'>. Line 1, Col: 28.
ParseError Required keyword: 'this' missing for <class 'sqlglot.expressions.query.Where'>. Line 1, Col: 26.
```

All three parse with `read="postgres"`, and quoting the name (`[output]`) works in T-SQL.

**Why it matters**

The T-SQL tokenizer maps `OUTPUT` to `TokenType.RETURNING` (`dialects/tsql.py`, `"OUTPUT": TokenType.RETURNING`), and `RETURNING` is not accepted as an identifier. So `output` can never be an unquoted column name in T-SQL. That name is common in real SQL Server code. `xp_cmdshell` returns its result in a column named `output`, so procedures that capture it typically do:

```sql
DECLARE @shell_output TABLE (output NVARCHAR(4000));
INSERT @shell_output EXEC xp_cmdshell @cmd;
DELETE @shell_output WHERE output IS NULL;
```

This statement runs as-is in our SQL Server production procedures, and sqlglot rejects it.

A related crash: with `error_level=ErrorLevel.IGNORE`, the same input yields a `Where(this=None)` tree, and `.sql("tsql")` on it raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'is_number'` (in `transforms.ensure_bools`). That may be expected for IGNORE-mode trees, so I mention it only for context.

**Expected**

`output` should parse as an identifier wherever it can't start an `OUTPUT` clause (select list, `WHERE`, `SET` targets, column definitions), the way other non-reserved keywords fall back to identifiers.

**Official documentation**

SQL Server's `xp_cmdshell` result set: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/system-stored-procedures/xp-cmdshell-transact-sql (the "Result sets" section shows the single `output` column).

tasks.issue:
Teradata: SAMPLE clause is transpiled to an empty TABLESAMPLE ()

**Before you file an issue**
- Read dialect: `teradata`
- Write dialect: any non-Teradata dialect (`snowflake`, `duckdb`, ...)
- Reproduced on `main` @ `9beb4ab28`

**Fully reproducible code snippet**

```python
import sqlglot

for sql in ("SELECT * FROM t SAMPLE 100", "SELECT * FROM t SAMPLE 0.25"):
    print(sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="teradata", write="snowflake")[0])
```

```
SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE ()
SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE ()
```

The Teradata parser stores the sample in `TableSample.expressions`, which other generators ignore, so the output is an empty `TABLESAMPLE ()` that doesn't parse. The same happens with `write="duckdb"`.

In Teradata an integer is a row count and a fraction is a proportion of rows, so the expected Snowflake output is:

| Teradata | Expected Snowflake |
|---|---|
| `SELECT * FROM t SAMPLE 100` | `SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE (100 ROWS)` |
| `SELECT * FROM t SAMPLE 0.25` | `SELECT * FROM t TABLESAMPLE (25)` |

**Official Documentation**
- https://docs.teradata.com/r/Enterprise_IntelliFlex_VMware/SQL-Data-Manipulation-Language/SELECT-Statements/SAMPLE-Clause/SAMPLE-Clause-Syntax
- https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/constructs/sample

tasks.title: MySQL XOR is parsed at AND precedence and optimizer folds a true expression to false
tasks.issue:
MySQL XOR is parsed at AND precedence and optimizer folds a true expression to false

## Summary and reproduction

With `sqlglot==30.23.0`:

```python
import sqlglot
from sqlglot.optimizer import optimize
query = "SELECT TRUE XOR FALSE AND FALSE"
print(optimize(sqlglot.parse_one(query, read="mysql"), dialect="mysql"))
```

Observed on 2026-10-19: `SELECT FALSE AS "_col_0"`. [MySQL binds `AND` above logical `XOR`](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/operator-precedence.html), so the source means `TRUE XOR (FALSE AND FALSE)` and is true. The observed fold corresponds to `(TRUE XOR FALSE) AND FALSE`, which is false.

The [MySQL parser configuration](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/ad8764a0436a7b5c500b783ebe50dbf20c1e477c/sqlglot/parsers/mysql.py#L72-L80) puts `XOR` in the `CONJUNCTION` tier alongside `AND`, so the parser builds the grouping that the optimizer folds to false.

trust.title: Snapshot leak checks
trust.detail: 0 of 40 test-set fixes and 0 of 40 fresh fixes are in the snapshots the setups learned from. The check does fire when it should: as positive controls it finds 24 of 40 dev fixes and 30 of 40 fresh fixes at HEAD.

trust.title: Fresh 2026 bugs
trust.detail: Half the tasks are bugs fixed in sqlglot between April and October 2026, mined directly from the repo. The agent sees only the linked GitHub issue.

trust.title: Dev and test kept apart
trust.detail: Setups were tuned on dev tasks only, and the code refuses any test or fresh task in the tuning inputs. Test and fresh tasks were used for this final report.

trust.title: A grader that fails closed
trust.detail: Only the repo's real tests decide a result, with test files reset first. Parsed results must match pytest's own summary, or the run can't pass. This caught 3 hidden-failure formats.

trust.title: Clean workspaces, one gap found and measured
trust.detail: Each run starts from one snapshot with no git history and without the repo's own CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, but the agent could still reach the web. Our audit of every tool call found 80 of 924 runs that reached the real fix or newer code, evenly across arms (12-16 per arm). Dropping every affected task leaves 51 tasks. No arm differs clearly from no setup on those tasks either.

trust.title: Every run metered
trust.detail: All 924 runs went through a hard-capped proxy that allows only Meta models. Its ledger total, $21.31, matches the sum of the runs' recorded costs.
